sources.entry: 🏙 The Paradox of Alerts: why deleting 90% of your paging alerts can make your systems better, and how to craft an on-call rotation that engineers are happy to join.

summary.title: The Paradox of Alerts
summary.one_liner: Deleting most symptom-based paging alerts in favor of SLO-based alerts, and building a humane on-call rotation, can make systems and engineers healthier.
takeaways: Delete paging alerts for symptoms such as high CPU or disk failure and alert on SLO burn, which tracks real user pain; this often cuts alert volume by over 90%.
Split non-urgent alerts into a second lane for daytime handling, and keep only a small set of trusted, documented paging alerts.
Track on-call health with measurable operational metrics like out-of-hours pages, deploy time, and failed deploys rather than hoping for no incidents.
Invest in observability (structured events, instrumentation, OpenTelemetry) and use it after every deploy so problems are found before users report them.
Use shadowing, buddies, safe blameless retros, and paid overtime or time off after bad nights to make on call sustainable.
summary.summary: This talk by Charity Majors argues that on-call pain should be aligned with real user pain, and that teams should remove most paging alerts in favor of SLO-based alerts. It covers alert lanes, documenting and tracking the few remaining pages, and running blameless retros to fix root causes. It also makes the case for observability over monitoring, auto-deploys, progressive delivery, and tracking team health metrics. The page is mostly slide-style bullet points with links, and it ends with advice to pay engineers a premium for out-of-hours alerts.
